name: Zinc oxide paste (Sudocrem)

card.summary: A British-Irish zinc-oxide barrier cream, sold over the counter for nappy rash, that people also dab on blemishes and irritated skin to calm and protect it.
card.note: Contains lanolin and benzyl compounds; a 2021 dermatology letter discusses dermatitis linked to the product.

quick.overview:
Sudocrem is a thick over-the-counter cream built on zinc oxide, lanolin and a water-repellent base. It was developed in Dublin in 1931 and is mainly sold to treat nappy rash, with other listed uses including eczema, minor burns, sunburn and surface wounds.

For appearance, it is used as a protective, calming layer on irritated or blemished skin, and UK and Irish media reported celebrities using it on acne from around 2012. Published studies of the product focus on dermatitis in incontinence and nappy rash rather than blemishes.
quick.how: A thin layer of the cream is spread over the irritated area; it is left on as a protective barrier. A related Sudocrem skin-care cream is marketed for everyday blemishes. People use it on spots, dry patches and irritated skin.
quick.risks: The cream contains lanolin and benzyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate and benzyl cinnamate. A 2021 letter in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology is titled 'Sudocrem dermatitis: easily missed'.

lead: Sudocrem is an over-the-counter medicated cream created in 1931 by Dublin pharmacist Thomas Smith, first as 'Smith's Cream' and then 'Soothing Cream', and named Sudocrem in 1950 [1]. By the 1960s samples given to new mothers built its popularity in Ireland, and it reached the UK in the 1970s [1]. It is now owned by Teva [1].

Its formulation (percent weight by weight) is zinc oxide 15.25, lanolin 4.00, benzyl benzoate 1.01, benzyl alcohol 0.39 and benzyl cinnamate 0.15 in a water-repellent base [1]. It is aimed mainly at irritant diaper dermatitis and also used for eczema, inverse psoriasis, pressure ulcers, minor burns, surface wounds, sunburn and chilblains [1].

The appearance angle is skin blemishes. Calming a red, irritated spot or patch makes the skin look more even, and a thick zinc-oxide layer is also used by some people as an overnight spot covering. Around 2012, Irish and UK media reported celebrities using Sudocrem for acne, and the manufacturer lists acne spots among the uses on its website and markets a Skin Care Cream as an everyday acne cream for young people [1][7]. Published trials of the product itself concern incontinence-associated dermatitis and nappy rash rather than blemishes [4][5][6].

Blemished or irritated skin looks calmer
angle.text: People use zinc-oxide barrier cream to calm irritated skin and spots. The product is marketed for nappy rash, with acne use promoted by media reports and a skin-care variant.

paras: Sudocrem is mainly used for irritant diaper dermatitis, with additional uses for eczema, inverse psoriasis, pressure ulcers, minor burns, wounds, sunburn and chilblains [1][2]. The manufacturer's UK website lists nappy rash, acne spots, eczema, cuts and grazes, minor burns, sunburn, pressure sores, incontinence-associated dermatitis and chafing, and describes the original cream as gentle enough to use from birth [7].

Irish and UK media reported around 2012 that celebrities used Sudocrem for acne, and a 2012 Irish Independent article, as summarized on Wikipedia, compared the cream to Irish staples after those reports [1]. The brand's UK range includes a Skin Care Cream described as an everyday acne cream aimed at young people [1][7]. Users describe dabbing the cream on individual spots or irritated patches and leaving it on as a protective layer. Wikipedia notes that the sources it cites do not include clinical evidence for acne treatment [1].

Wikipedia lists three UK variants: Original Antiseptic Healing Cream, Care and Protect (a nappy rash preventative) and Skin Care Cream [1]. The manufacturer's site also lists Sudosalve for broken, inflamed nappy rash, My Little Sudocrem, Sudocrem Naturals and Assuraderm, and states that the formulation contains no animal-derived ingredients [7]. The cream is sold as Dermocrem in Belgium; the Netherlands was the first market outside Ireland and the UK, and it is also sold in Malaysia [1].

Zinc oxide acts as an astringent and protective agent, lanolin as an emollient, and benzyl alcohol as a mild anaesthetic and disinfectant; benzyl cinnamate is described as antibacterial and antifungal [1]. The base is water-repellent, so the cream forms a barrier on the skin [2].

Zinc oxide itself is used widely in skin care: Wikipedia lists its use in diaper rash creams, calamine, barrier creams and antiseptic ointments, and as a photostable UVA and UVB sunscreen filter approved by the FDA [8]. The same article describes zinc oxide as non-irritating and non-comedogenic and notes that skin absorption is slight [8].

Smith developed the cream in 1931 in Dublin. It was renamed in 1950, spread through samples to mothers in the 1960s, and reached the UK in the 1970s [1]. The manufacturer says it has been trusted for over 90 years and cites a February 2015 survey of 2,159 respondents for its claim to be the UK's number one nappy rash brand [7].

Forest Laboratories Europe made the product until 2014, when Actavis plc acquired and merged the business; Actavis later bought Allergan, and Teva acquired Actavis in 2016 [1]. Production moved from Baldoyle to Bulgaria, with Teva announcing in May 2021 that the Dublin plant would close and production would shift to Troyan by 2023, citing rising international demand [1].

The cream contains lanolin and benzyl compounds, which are known contact allergens. A 2021 letter in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology is titled 'Sudocrem dermatitis: easily missed', indicating that the product has been associated with dermatitis in some patients [3]. The manufacturer asks that adverse events be reported to Teva UK Limited and advises reading the label [7].

A double-blind randomized trial in elderly inpatients found Sudocrem superior to zinc cream BP for treating incontinence-associated dermatitis, with no significant difference for prevention [4]. A 1999 randomized trial compared eosin with zinc oxide paste and corticosteroid cream for diaper dermatitis [5]. A 2016 real-world evidence study evaluated a treatment for nappy rash [6]. No trials of Sudocrem for acne or blemishes are listed.

timeline.event: Thomas Smith develops the cream in Dublin [1].
Samples given to new mothers in Ireland build its popularity [1].
Irish and UK media report celebrities using it for acne [1].
Actavis acquires manufacturer Forest Laboratories Europe [1].
Teva announces closure of the Baldoyle plant and a move to Troyan, Bulgaria [1].
